##### SECTION 1:  INTRODUCTION 

In this report we provide an Executive Summary which gives an overview of the main issues in the outlook for the copper industry.  A brief outline of our approach in forecasting output and the main definitions are provided below. 

###### Note on Methodology 

In the supply analysis, forecasts of mine and smelter production to 2020 are composed of three elements; firstly, “ **base case** ” production capability or capacity; secondly, **highly probable projects** ; and thirdly, a further **production adjustment** . 

- **Base case production capability or capacity** comprises existing operations, along with expansions or greenfield projects that are under construction or that have received board approval and that have been financed. 

- **Highly probable projects** do not meet these strict criteria for inclusion as base case capacity but, in Brook Hunt’s judgement, will most likely proceed within the time frame indicated. 

- In order to maintain an orderly market a **production adjustment** is made taking into account price levels, industry cost st

ructure, concentrate availability, TC/RCs etc.  Where the production adjustment is positive, i.e. there is a need for further mine/smelter/refinery production over and above base case and highly probable output, implicit reference is made to the existence of other projects, both probable and possible, in order to assess whether there are enough projects sufficiently far advanced in their exploration/development to fill the potential supply gap.  If base case plus highly probable supply is expected to exceed forecast demand, then a _negative_ adjustment to output may be made in order to prevent the build up of unrealistically large inventories.  Typically, lower prices will be the catalyst for this action and will be reflected in the market forecast.  Reference is made to the industry cost structure to determine the likely level of production loss at specific price levels.

##### SECTION 2:  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 

- Global demand for copper has been severely impacted by the downturn in manufacturing activity and destocking.  After growing by a modest 2.7% to 17.9Mt in 2007, global copper consumption contracted by 0.2% in 2008 to just below 17.9Mt.  However, this year we are forecasting that consumption will decline by 3.5% to ~17.3Mt.  The bulk of the contraction is forecast to occur in the world’s mature economies where consumption is forecast to fall by 12.5% to 6.1Mt. 

- During the current price cycle, which is projected to run from 2002 to 2010, we forecast that global consumption will grow at an average rate of 2% p.a.  During the remainder of the forecast period (2010-2020) we believe that global refined copper consumption will grow by 3.5% p.a. The stronger rate in the latter period (2010-2020) partly reflects continued healthy demand from Russia and China, as their economies continue to develop, as well as robust demand from both India and Brazil. 

- We forecast that base case mine production capability will increase by 3.9% this year to ~16.2Mt.  Previously we were forecasting a gain of 3.5% to 16.1Mt.  Between 2002 and 2010 (the current price cycle) the average annual growth rate in base case world copper mine production capability (excluding highly probable and probable projects) is forecast to be 2.3% p.a., including 2.1% p.a. ex-concentrates and 3.3% p.a from SxEw sources. 

- Based on current production plans, the general trend in base case mine production capability is for a decline from 2013 onwards as production is lost, either to mine closures, or grade attrition exceeding committed incremental expansion or committed new project capacity.  Base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 1.3% p.a. between 2010 (inclusive) and 2020 with mine output falling from a peak of ~17.6Mt in 2012 to ~14Mt in 2020.  At the same time, demand for additional mine production to meet increased market requirements for refined metal will create an implied shortfall in mine

output of ~1.3Mt/a in 2013, 3.9Mt/a in 2016 and 7.6Mt/a by 2020. 

- We expect base case global copper smelter production capability to reach 14.6Mt/a in 2009 (+1.7%), rising to ~16.4Mt in 2010 (+12.8%) and 17.6Mt in 2011 (+6.8%).  During the current price cycle (20022010) base case global smelter production capability is forecast to rise at a rate of 3.4% p.a. before falling to 2.2% p.a. during the period 20102020. 

- Our forecast global market surplus now stands at ~585kt for the year. This is little changed for our previous surplus estimate of 515kt and stocks, at 63 days of consumption, have returned to more normal levels of 60-65 days.  Nevertheless, we have raised our average price forecast for the year, lifting it from $3636/t ($1.65/lb) previously to $4186/t. The 15% gain in price reflects a much stronger than anticipated price environment for the year so far, especially during Q2, brought about by much healthier than expected Chinese demand. 

- We forecast that global industrial production growth will average 3.1% p.a. over the period 2009-2020.  Mature economy IP is expected to grow by an average of just 1.2% p.a over the period while developing IP is forecast to increase by a much stronger 6.4% p.a.

##### SECTION 3:  DEMAND ANALYSIS 

###### Changes to demand forecasts since Q1. 

The collapse in economic activity, which began in Q3 last year, has been exacerbated by savage destocking at all levels of the global consumption chain. This, in turn, has continued to have a dramatic impact on global copper demand (ex China) throughout Q2.  However, the destocking process is now showing tentative signs to suggest that it may be coming to an end, with inventories now more closely aligned to demand.  In some cases there have been some indications of restocking.  However, with end-user demand still at extremely low levels restocking will be minimal.  Many consumers are adjusting inventories on a week-to-week basis to ensure that they have material to meet their work-inhand needs.  Nevertheless, any further deterioration in demand will force further destocking.  The level or uncertainty surrounding demand is so high that inventories will be very tightly managed throughout 2009 and well into 2010. Also, continued tightness of credit will exacerbate the situation further. 

The scale of the downturn in global manufacturing activity was highlighted by the decline witnessed in the purchasing managers’ index surveys for manufacturing in the world’s major economies.  During the initial phase of the downturn (Q4 2008) the PMI’s for the US, EU, Japan, China and India all slid below the 50 level, the threshold between growth and contraction.  Since then only the manufacturing sectors of China and India have climbed back above the 50 level (see chart below).  This is in stark contrast the PMI’s of the world’s mature economies which remain well below 50 at levels that are still comparable

to those seen at the bottom of the 2001 recession. In the wake of the 2001 recession it took 24 months for the PMIs to sustainably climb above the 50 level. If the manufacturing sector of world’s mature economies mirror a similar recovery path this time, a sustained recovery in manufacturing is unlikely to emerge until second half of 2010 at the earliest. The effects of China’s $585 Bn stimulus package are starting to be felt with fixed asset investment in the first five months of the year rising by 32.9%, an acceleration from the 30.5% increase seen in the first four months of the year. Since the stimulus package was announced in November some 20,000 km of rural roads have been built, 445km of highway, 100,000 m2 of airport buildings, 214,000 units of low income housing has been completed and construction of a further 650,000 units has begun. In rural areas 30,000 km of new power lines and 254 electrical substations have also been built. The construction of several major railroad projects has also been accelerated with spending on the sector rising by 110% in the first five months of the year. A further near-term boost to growth is coming from the huge increase in bank lending. New loans rose by more than double in the first five months of the year, rising from RMB319 Bn to RMB665 Bn. This vast increase in lending has provided China’s industry with a ready source of funds for capacity increases a

nd additional liquidity if needed. However, in the medium- to long-term, the impact of such an increase in credit raises the spectre of inflating asset bubbles, creating excess industrial capacity and an increase in bad debts for the country’s banks. One impact of the increased lending has been a sharp increase in house sales in China’s coastal provinces. Sales in Shanghai in the first five months of the year rose by 62%, those in Beijing doubled and the eastern region as a whole saw a 54% increase. However, despite the increase in sales, prices many cities fell in May, in Beijing they were 1.1% lower, and in Shanghai they fell by 1.6%. The continued falls in prices, despite the increase in sales volumes suggests that oversupply is still a major problem in China’s coastal provinces and that the increased availability of credit may be fuelling a speculative boom. n economies continue to suffer from falling export demand for the region’s manufactured goods, weak construction sectors and an uncoordinated and disparate policy response from the continent’s governments.  As a result the European experience of the downturn will be more painful and sustained than in the US. 

Germany has been one of the biggest victims of the downturn, with previously ebullient export demand for high technology consumer and capital goods evaporating since the downturn bit in the last quarter of 2008.  As a consequence German industrial production has shown double digit declines in year-on-year terms since December 2008 and in April it fell by 21.6%.  Such deep contractions in activity suggest that the outlook for the German manufacturing sector is extremely poor, particularly in light of its reliance on exports of capital goods, demand for which typically lags any economic recovery. 

One of the measures that the German Government has undertaken is a car scrapping scheme whereby owners can apply for a €2500 grant towards a new car if they scrap one that is nine years old or more.  The scheme has been a resounding success in that German car sales in the first four months of the year totalled 1.25M units, a year-on-year rise of 27%.  However, this rise in sales has not boosted production which has fallen by 30% to 1.38M units over the same period.  Meanwhile, commercial vehicle sales, which are not beneficiaries of the scrapping scheme, have fallen annually by 23% in the first nine months of the year. 

While the scrapping scheme seems to be helping German automakers keep inventories down, it is also delaying an inevitable slowdown in sales.  The scheme is scheduled to finish at the end of this year and once this occurs sales in 2010 are likely to slump.  Furthermore, future car sales could be depressed for several years because the scheme has effectively reduced the age of the German car fleet and cut the near- to medium-term demand for new cars. 

Despite the strong growth in German car sales, sales of cars across Europe as a whole have fallen for 13 consecutive months.  According to the European Automobile Manufacturers Association sales in May fell by 4.9% in year-on-year terms, the slide is a marginal improvement on the double digit declines that we have seen in recent months.  Having said that, May 2008’s sales figure was itself 8% lower than a year earlier.  Sales for the first five months of the year totalled 5.8M units, a year-on-year decline of 14.7%.  Meanwhile, European car production totalled 4.7M units, a year-on-year decline of 27%.

The manufacturing PMI for the European Union fell to a low of just 33.99 in February, some 22% lower than the level reached at the bottom of the 2001 recession. There are some signs of encouragement with the PMI subsequently posting a strong recovery rising to 41.44 in May, the new orders sub-index has also recovered climbing from December’s low of 27.19 to 43.25 and with inventories at such low levels the pickup in new orders raises the possibility of a slight boost to manufacturing output because of restocking. However, with the main index remaining well below the 50 level, which separates contraction in the manufacturing sector from expansion, any recovery in manufacturing remains many months away – in the last recession the Eurozone PMI took 24 months before there was a sustained period of the PMI climbing above 50. The situation in the European construction sector is equally bad. In its latest estimates the European federation of construction research institutes, Euroconstruct, estimates that major contractions will occur in the construction sectors of most European countries. With output in 2008 falling by 3.1%, total construction output in 2009 is forecast to contract by a further 7.5% and in 2010 a fall of 1% is forecast. The sector as a whole is not forecast to return to growth until 2011 with an increase of 1.6%. Unusually, the contraction is forecast to affect all of the main construction sectors including civil engineering. The greatest weakness is forecast for the residential sector with contractions of 61%, 42%, 40% and 30% forecast for Ireland, Spain, Denmark and Sweden respectively The contraction in manufacturing and construction activity has had a devastating impact on demand for copper and copper alloy products throughout the region. The company did not provide a product output breakdown but it did report that demand for brass rods used in plumbing was hit the hardest. This was not surprising in light of the slowdown in the European construction sector. In contrast, demand for products used in the power generation industry, especially in renewable energy generation, was more resilient. ###### Scrap Definition 

_Copper scrap is classified into two categories_ 

Copper scrap is classified into two general categories called old and new scrap. New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply.  A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles.  New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which do

es not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. 

###### **Scrapping Rates** 

_Old scrap availability is linked to the volume of copper containing products_ 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in nonelectrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

###### **Scrap Usage** 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

_Some products can contain higher amounts of scrap than others_ 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases.

###### Europe 

The key European economies – Germany, the UK, France and Italy, are now contracting rapidly.  Overall, growth in the third largest economic region will contract by 3.9% in 2009. This may be because household wealth in Germany has been somewhat protected by a relatively stable German housing market.
